prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, through the conception, construction and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider

statement.case_for: The Higgs discovery is the clearest uncredited experimental milestone on the shortlist. Two independent detectors observed the same new boson in 2012, the 2013 prize covered only the theoretical mechanism, and more than a decade of coupling, mass and spin-parity measurements has made the result stable. It is a discovery in the sense that should sit at the centre of the prize, and four of eight members opened it in first place. The three-person limit forces a choice, and I keep a configuration that is balanced across the two experiments: Gianotti and Jenni for ATLAS and Virdee for CMS. This covers the leadership at the time of the announcement and the founding-era leadership of ATLAS, and it keeps one credited name from each collaboration's technical and organisational core.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness. Thousands of people contributed, any three names are a judgement about leadership versus decisive technical work, and a prize for the Higgs observation will look arbitrary to many in the community whoever is chosen. Four names are credited and only three can be used, so one of Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee or Gianotti must be left out. There is also an argument that the committee should prefer a discovery with a cleaner two- or three-person structure, such as optical lattice clocks, rather than adjudicate a collaboration-scale credit dispute.

responses.point: Johansson proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, which gives two ATLAS names and one CMS founder, and acknowledges that this omits Virdee and leaves the balance between the two experiments contestable.
responses.response: I accept that this is a judgement call, and I do not claim my trio is uniquely correct. I still prefer to keep Virdee over Della Negra. Virdee was CMS spokesperson around the time of the discovery and a central figure in the construction of the CMS calorimetry, whereas Della Negra's role was concentrated in the founding years of the collaboration. Giving two of the three places to ATLAS is an asymmetry that I would resist unless the committee has a clear reason to value ATLAS leadership above CMS. I would be willing to move to Della Negra if colleagues convince me that founding conception should outweigh leadership at the time of the discovery.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs first with Gianotti, Della Negra and Virdee, argues that instrument-driven discovery is compelling, and puts the IceCube neutrino observation second.
responses.response: I share the view that the Higgs is the clearest experimental milestone and that attribution is a leadership judgement rather than a verified accounting. Where I disagree is on IceCube as a close second. I ranked it fourth because the diffuse flux is secure but the source picture (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) is still developing, and Halzen, Karle and Spiering would be honoured for a discovery whose physical interpretation is not yet settled. I would rather wait for the source population to be understood. Your balance of two CMS names and one ATLAS name is the mirror image of Johansson's, which shows how little the supplied text can settle the question.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because the concept is clear, the realisation is decisive, the precision of about 1e-18 is unmatched and the Katori and Ye attribution is natural.
responses.response: I agree that B013 is the cleanest case on the shortlist in terms of attribution and I ranked it second; every member ranked it in the top four, which is notable. My reservation is only about the framing: Ye's link to the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the earlier ion-clock recognition in 2012 make this a continuation of a metrology line already honoured, while the Higgs experimental discovery has never been recognised. The redefinition of the second is also still pending, so the clock case may gain further strength with time, whereas the Higgs case will not. I regard B013 as the right fallback if the committee cannot agree on a Higgs trio.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the topological insulator entry third and notes that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are the most coherent theory-plus-experiment set among the supplied names, although the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang leaves a significant gap.
responses.response: I ranked B044 third for the same reason and I agree with your assessment of the credit gap. I would add that the gap is more serious than a footnote: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang identified the HgTe route that Molenkamp's group then realised, and Zhang's death rules out the one person whose recognition would have been the most natural. The overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize also makes me hesitate. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would be defensible, but I would not put it above the Higgs or the clocks while the attribution question is open.

responses.point: Mehlig supports the Higgs in first place with Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, and states that any three-person choice is partly arbitrary and that the experimental recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I agree that recognition is overdue and I endorse your candour about the arbitrariness. I would add one qualification to the reading of the opening support: four first places for B001 reflect agreement on the discovery, not agreement on the names. Gianotti appears in all seven proposals, but Della Negra appears in five, Jenni in five and Virdee in four, so the second and third places are genuinely open. The committee should therefore settle on the names through the attribution argument and not through a count of proposals.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a leadership-based trio for a collaboration-scale discovery, and whether it prefers conception and construction leadership or leadership at the time of the discovery.
Which of Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee should take the third and second places. I rely on general knowledge of their roles that the supplied text does not settle.
Whether the 2012 and 2005 prizes in related metrology make B013 a less appealing alternative than its high ranking across the committee suggests.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My connections are David Gross (PhD supervisor), Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none of them is a credited name on the shortlisted ballots.
